projects.title: MCU Data Logger
projects.intro: An ATmega328P data-logging board with dual I²C EEPROMs and a real-time clock. A compact two-layer design, from schematic to fabrication package.
projects.status: Rev A layout complete · electrical checks passed
projects.caption: Rev A · KiCad render of the final routed board · hardware bring-up pending

sections.title: The challenge
sections.text: Develop a compact microcontroller board with nonvolatile storage, timekeeping, accessible interfaces, and programming connections for future data-logging firmware.

sections.title: Engineering work
sections.text: ATmega328P-AUR in TQFP-32, two 24LC1025 I²C EEPROMs, a DS1337 RTC, and separate 16 MHz and 32.768 kHz crystals. UART, I²C, GPIO, and a 2×3 ISP header expose the development interfaces in an approximately 52.1 × 34.9 mm two-layer board.

sections.title: Verification
sections.text: KiCad reports zero DRC violations, zero unconnected pads, zero footprint/parity errors, and zero schematic ERC errors or warnings. The final board includes a filled B.Cu ground zone, explicit manufacturing rules, and wider power traces where clearance permits.

sections.title: Design completion & next steps
sections.text: Gerber and drill files are generated from the verified board. This is a hardware CAD and fabrication package; firmware development, board assembly, power-up checks, and physical performance testing remain bring-up work.

projects.detailCaption: Final top and bottom fabrication views, rendered from exported Gerber and Excellon files. Bottom view is mirrored for viewing from the back.

codeSnapshots.caption: Actual KiCad CAD source: the bottom-copper GND zone and thermal-relief parameters. Layout source, not data-logging firmware.

projects.title:
STM32H7
photoacoustics.
projects.intro: An STM32H7 acquisition platform for pulsed-LED photoacoustic tomography. Research into the timing, buffering, and interfaces behind useful signals.
projects.caption: Development architecture · proposed data path, not a validated end-to-end system

sections.title: Research context
sections.text: Developing a microcontroller-based acquisition platform for pulsed-LED photoacoustic tomography at Iowa State University, working with Prof. Manojit Pramanik.

sections.title: My focus
sections.text: Timer-triggered ADC sampling, DMA-to-RAM buffering, memory organization, and peripheral integration. The design work explores how timing and data movement constrain an embedded acquisition pipeline.

sections.title: System direction
sections.text: The development plan connects STM32H7 acquisition to a planned ESP32 gateway and host interface. MCU selection and end-to-end integration remain development decisions.

sections.title: Current evidence
sections.text: Ongoing research documented in my resume and development plan. No completed tomography reconstruction, measured throughput, or end-to-end hardware validation is claimed here.

projects.title:
Power systems.
Human interfaces.
projects.intro: ESP32 display and Flutter prototypes for power-system telemetry. From a wired bench display to a mobile interface for monitoring and commands.
projects.caption: Original IIT Hyderabad report photograph and PPS Monitor screenshot

sections.title: The challenge
sections.text: Make power-system information usable on small embedded screens and mobile devices: clear values, responsive graphs, and accessible controls across different communication paths.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.text: Built ESP32 TFT interfaces with selective redraw, debounced buttons, scrolling graph buffers, and touch calibration. Developed Flutter views for telemetry, graphing, and command interactions.

sections.title: Implementation
sections.text: The report describes W5500 Ethernet, Bluetooth Classic, BLE, and later Wi-Fi variants. The public Flutter code implements BLE discovery, WebSocket transport, six-field telemetry parsing, rolling plots, and control messages.

sections.title: Evidence & limits
sections.text: The public ESP32 firmware generates simulated readings and logs received commands. It demonstrates communications and interface behavior, not calibrated power measurements or physical closed-loop regulation. The touchscreen prototype also used a potentiometer as an analog input.

projects.detailCaption: Original report screenshot: PPS Monitor graph interface. Displayed values are not presented as independently verified measurements.

codeSnapshots.caption: Actual Flutter source: keep a bounded history for each telemetry metric, then append a point to its plot. The companion public firmware supplies simulated readings.

projects.title:
Four ESP32s.
One dashboard.
projects.intro: Four ESP32 boards, each connected through W5500 Ethernet, stream generated waveforms into one Flutter dashboard. Independent connections, four graph panels, and per-device recording.
projects.caption: Original report photographs of the four-panel Flutter dashboard: upper and lower views. Each graph belongs to an independent ESP32/W5500 connection.

sections.title: Four independent data streams
sections.text: Built a Flutter visualizer supporting four ESP32 boards with W5500 Ethernet modules. Each board runs its own WebSocket server on port 81 and streams mathematically generated sine-wave data to a separate graph.

sections.title: My contribution
sections.text: Maintained four independent WebSocketChannel instances with separate listeners, editable device IPs, connection status, and a CustomPainter graph per ESP32. Added per-device recording and clipboard-based CSV export. Generated waveforms exercise communication and visualization; they are not measured sensor signals.

sections.title: Another four-board experiment
sections.text: The report also documents four ESP32 boards and four W5500 modules arranged as three senders and one receiver. Sender IDs determine priority, with ESP1 ranked above ESP2 and ESP3.

sections.title: Report evidence
sections.text: The report documents the four-channel dashboard and records successful sender connections and priority-based acceptance/rejection in the separate messaging experiment. It does not establish hardware clock synchronization, fault-tolerant failover, or a validated latency benchmark.
